mcqs.question: What was the key architectural shift from 3G to 4G/LTE, beyond just higher speed?
options: 4G/LTE moved to an all-IP network, carrying voice itself as data (VoLTE) rather than a separate circuit-switched voice channel
4G introduced cell towers for the first time; 3G had none
4G eliminated the need for handoffs between towers
4G was purely a marketing rebrand of 3G with no technical differences
mcqs.explanation: The all-IP shift, including voice becoming data via VoLTE, is the concrete architectural change. Cell towers predate 4G, handoffs remain necessary in every generation, and the technical differences between generations are substantial, not cosmetic.

mcqs.question: Why can a cell tower handoff sometimes break a device's ongoing TCP connection, even though the mobility management itself succeeded?
options: TCP connections are tied to a specific cell tower's hardware ID, not IP address
The handoff can change the device's IP address, and TCP identifies a connection by the IP/port 4-tuple, so a changed IP breaks the existing connection
Handoffs always terminate every active connection by design, regardless of protocol
Cellular networks don't support TCP at all, only UDP
mcqs.explanation: TCP's IP/port-based connection identity is exactly why an IP change from a handoff can break it, even when the radio-level handoff itself worked fine. TCP doesn't key off tower hardware IDs, handoffs don't always kill connections by design, and cellular networks fully support TCP.

mcqs.question: A factory wants to deploy thousands of low-power IoT sensors per site on a cellular connection. Which 5G pillar is most relevant?
options: URLLC, since it only concerns encryption strength
eMBB, since it's focused on consumer video streaming throughput
mMTC (Massive Machine-Type Communications), designed for extremely high device density per cell
None — 5G's pillars only apply to smartphones
mcqs.explanation: mMTC is specifically the pillar built for massive device density, which matches this use case directly. eMBB targets consumer throughput, URLLC targets latency/reliability rather than encryption, and 5G's pillars explicitly extend beyond smartphones.

mcqs.question: An app performs perfectly in testing on office Wi-Fi but times out frequently for cellular users under normal (not faulty) conditions. What's the likely root cause?
options: Cellular networks are fundamentally incompatible with the TCP protocol
The app's server is only reachable from Wi-Fi networks
The app's timeouts and assumptions were tuned for stable wired/Wi-Fi latency, and don't account for cellular's inherently higher and more variable latency and loss
mcqs.explanation: Mistuned assumptions about latency and jitter are the realistic root cause for this pattern. Cellular networks fully support TCP, server reachability isn't tied to the client's access type, and there's no general 5G throttling of third-party apps.
